Clinical Vignette

Patient: Female, 69, Agricultural Worker, Married

Edna has worked the land for most of her life. She and her husband, Gerald, have farmed the same stretch of valley in rural Ontario for over forty years, growing field corn and soybeans, raising a few cattle, living by the rhythm of seasons. She is a practical woman — broad-shouldered, plain-spoken, the kind of person who gets up before dawn without complaint and considers endurance a virtue. She has never thought of herself as someone who falls apart.

Two years ago, during a late-October harvest, Edna was sexually assaulted by a contract worker her husband had hired to help bring in the crop. Gerald had driven into town for parts. She was alone in the equipment shed when it happened. She did not tell her husband that night. She did not tell anyone for nearly four months. She cleaned herself up, went inside, started dinner, and when Gerald came home she said she had a headache and went to bed early. She lay in the dark and listened to the combines in the neighboring fields and felt, she later described, like something had been taken out of her that she could not name.

The silence did not protect her the way she had hoped. In the weeks that followed, she found herself unable to enter the equipment shed without her chest seizing. She began routing her daily work around it, adding unnecessary distance to her mornings, offering Gerald vague excuses. At night she slept in fragments, waking at two or three in the morning with her heart pounding, certain she had heard footsteps in the yard. She would lie rigid beside her sleeping husband, listening, not waking him, not wanting to explain what she could barely explain to herself.

Spring planting came and she worked through it, but she was not the same woman in the field. She startled badly at sounds — a tractor backfiring, a door swinging shut in the wind. She began to avoid the hired hands Gerald brought on seasonally, finding reasons to stay in the house when they were near. She stopped attending the agricultural co-op meetings she had gone to for thirty years. Gerald noticed she had become quieter, more withdrawn, and assumed it was her age, or her knees, which had been giving her trouble. She let him believe that.

She told her daughter the truth first, over the phone, in February of this year, crying in a way she describes as shameful — ugly, uncontrolled. Her daughter drove up from Guelph and sat with her for a weekend and eventually persuaded her to see someone. Coming to therapy was not something Edna would have chosen on her own. She sat in the first session with her coat still on and her hands folded in her lap, apologizing for taking up time.

Now, several sessions in, the shape of her inner life has become clearer. She carries a persistent, corrosive belief that she should have fought harder, screamed, done something different. She replays the assault in involuntary flashes — the smell of diesel and cold metal, the particular quality of the afternoon light through the shed's high window — and these images arrive without warning, while she is seeding, while she is cooking, while she is sitting beside Gerald watching the evening news. She feels profoundly disconnected from the woman she was before, as though that person belongs to someone else's life. She describes herself as numb to things that used to matter — the first thaw, the smell of turned earth, the satisfaction of a good yield. These were once the anchors of her identity. She reaches for them now and finds very little there.

She still gets up before dawn. She still does the work. But she moves through her days with a wariness that does not lift, scanning the yard before she steps outside, checking locks she never used to check, waiting — though she cannot say for what — for something else to go wrong.
